name: Down Street
fact: Churchill used the tunnels as a Cabinet War Room during the Blitz before moving to Whitehall. The platform is sealed but largely intact.

name: Brompton Road
fact: Closed due to low passenger numbers. The surface building became an anti-aircraft gun operations centre in WWII and is now used by the MoD.

name: Aldwych
fact: Closed as uneconomic — just 450 passengers used it daily. The BBC has filmed here so often that the platform is instantly recognisable from dozens of films.

name: Charing Cross (Jubilee)
fact: Closed when the Jubilee line was extended eastward to Stratford. The tunnels and platforms remain sealed beneath the Strand.

name: British Museum
fact: Closed because Holborn station was so close. The 1935 film Bulldog Jack featured a fictional ghost train from this station — the urban legend spread further than the truth.

name: York Road
fact: Used only by workers at the nearby goods depot. The station building still stands on York Way, now converted to residential use.

name: South Kentish Town
fact: A passenger was once stranded here after accidentally exiting at the wrong station — the lifts were already being decommissioned and he had to be rescued by Underground staff.

name: Marlborough Road
fact: Replaced by the adjacent St John's Wood station. The building on Queen's Grove has been converted to private use and retains its Leslie Green oxblood terracotta facade.

name: City Road
fact: One of the original 1901 City & South London Railway stations. Closed during post-WWI reconstruction works and never reopened. The building has since been demolished.

name: King William Street
fact: The original southern terminus of the world's first deep-level electric tube railway, opened 1890. Its awkward curved approach was why it closed — trains could barely navigate the bend.

name: Shoreditch
fact: Closed when the East London line was handed to London Overground. The station's Brutalist surface building became a pop-up venue space much loved by the neighbourhood it once served.

name: Ongar
fact: The most remote station in TfL history — 35 miles from central London, served by a steam locomotive on a branch that ran through open countryside. Now a heritage railway.

name: Bull & Bush (never opened)
fact: Construction was completed in 1906 but the station was never opened to passengers. The tunnels exist beneath Hampstead Heath. Part of the unfinished Charing Cross, Euston & Hampstead Railway extension.

name: Wood Lane
fact: Original name for what is now Latimer Road. The 1908 station opened for the Franco-British Exhibition and remained in use for 51 years before being superseded.
